Snapchat Scam UK: How to Spot Fake Messages and Protect Your Account

Snapchat scammers use fake support messages and social engineering to steal passwords, payment details, and money — but you can spot and stop them.

By Alex Bacsa · Published 2026-08-08 · 8 min read

Key rule: verify through an official route you opened yourself, not the link, number, app, or payment details supplied by the suspicious message.

Being targeted right now? Do this

  1. Stop. Don’t pay, transfer money, or share passwords, PINs, or one-time codes.
  2. Contact your bank on the number on the back of your card if your money or details may be at risk.
  3. Use the right recovery route. Follow the payment, account and identity checklist; reporting differs in Scotland.

The main Snapchat scams targeting UK users

Snapchat scams in the UK fall into several overlapping patterns. The most common is the fake support message — scammers send a direct message or email claiming to be Snapchat support, saying your account has been locked, flagged for suspicious activity, or will be deleted unless you verify your identity immediately. They include a link to a fake login page designed to steal your username and password.

A second major pattern is romance and investment fraud: scammers build relationships with users over weeks or months, then ask for money for an emergency, a business opportunity, or to 'unlock' a supposed investment. A third involves fake Snapchat gift card or payment offers — messages claiming you've won a reward or can buy discounted Snapchat+ subscriptions, which lead to phishing pages or payment scams. All three exploit the app's speed and the trust users place in messages from accounts that look official or belong to people they think they know.

Warning signs of a Snapchat scam message

  • **Urgent language and threats of account deletion.** Genuine Snapchat support will not threaten to delete your account in a direct message or demand immediate action. They give you time to respond through official channels.
  • **A link to 'verify' or 'confirm' your identity.** Real Snapchat support will never ask you to click a link in a message to log in again. If your account needs attention, Snapchat will notify you in the app itself or via your registered email address.
  • **Requests for your password, two-factor authentication code, or recovery email.** Snapchat staff will never ask for these details in a message. No legitimate company asks for passwords via direct message.
  • **Misspelled Snapchat branding or odd usernames.** Scammers often use accounts with names like 'snapchat-support' or 'snapchat_help' instead of the official Snapchat account. Check the username carefully.
  • **Messages from people you don't know asking for money or personal details.** Romance and investment scams often start with friendly conversation before pivoting to requests for cash or sensitive information.
  • **Offers of free or heavily discounted Snapchat+ or gift cards.** Scammers use these to lure you to fake payment pages or to build trust before asking for larger sums.
  • **Poor grammar or spelling in official-looking messages.** Snapchat's real support communications are professionally written. Awkward phrasing is a red flag.
  • **Requests to move the conversation to another app or platform.** Scammers often ask you to switch to WhatsApp, Telegram, or email to avoid Snapchat's moderation and to isolate you from safety features.

How Snapchat scams work from first contact to loss

A typical Snapchat scam begins with a message that appears urgent and official. If it's a fake support scam, the message claims your account is at risk and includes a link. You click it, land on a page that looks almost identical to Snapchat's real login screen, and enter your username and password. The scammer now has your credentials and can log in, change your password, access your saved photos and messages, and potentially link a payment method to your account.

If it's a romance or investment scam, the process is slower: a scammer builds rapport over days or weeks, shares a convincing story (a business opportunity, a medical emergency, a way to 'unlock' profits), and asks you to send money via bank transfer, gift card, or cryptocurrency. Once the money is sent, it is extremely difficult to recover. If it's a fake gift card or payment offer, you click a link, enter your payment details on a fake checkout page, and the scammer either charges your card directly or uses your details for fraud elsewhere.

In all cases, the scammer's goal is to extract money, steal your identity, or compromise your account to target your contacts next.

How to check if a Snapchat message is really from Snapchat

Snapchat's official support account on the app is verified with a badge and has the username 'snapchat'. If you receive a message claiming to be from support, open your Snapchat app and search for the official Snapchat account to compare. The real account will have a blue verified badge next to the name. Do not click any links in unsolicited messages. Instead, if you're concerned about your account, open Snapchat directly (not via a link) and go to Settings > Help > Contact Us to reach genuine support.

Snapchat will never ask you to log in again via a link in a message — if there's a security issue, the app will prompt you to take action when you open it. Check the sender's username carefully: scammers use similar-looking names like 'snapchat_support' or 'snapchat-help'. For romance or investment offers, search the person's name and photo on Google Images or reverse image search to see if they appear elsewhere online under different identities — a common sign of a catfish.

If someone you've just met is pushing you to move to a private chat app or asking for money, that is almost always a scam. Genuine Snapchat staff will never ask for your password, recovery email, or two-factor authentication code.

What to do immediately if you've clicked a scam link or shared details

If you entered your Snapchat password on a fake login page, change your password right now using the official Snapchat app or website. Go to Settings > Username > Password and create a new, strong password that you haven't used elsewhere. If you've already changed your password and the scammer has not locked you out, enable two-factor authentication in Settings > Two-Factor Authentication to add an extra layer of security. Check your account activity: go to Settings > Login Activity to see if anyone else has accessed your account from an unfamiliar location or device.

If you see suspicious activity, log out all other sessions. If you shared your recovery email or phone number, consider changing the password on that email account too, as the scammer may try to use it to reset your Snapchat password. If you sent money via bank transfer, contact your bank immediately and explain that you've been scammed; they may be able to recall the payment if it hasn't been withdrawn. If you used a gift card or credit card, report it to your card issuer and ask them to cancel the card and issue a replacement.

Do not send any more money or information to the scammer, and do not respond to further messages.

Reporting Snapchat scams in the UK

Report the scam to Snapchat directly: open the message, tap the three dots, and select 'Report'. This helps Snapchat remove the fake account and protect other users. If the scam involved a phishing link (a fake login page), report it to the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) Suspicious Email Reporting Service at report@phishing.gov.uk — include the link and any details about how you found it. If you received a scam SMS or text message, forward it to 7726 (spells 'SPAM').

For financial loss or identity theft, report the scam to Report Fraud (0300 123 2040, https://www.reportfraud.police.uk) if you are in England, Wales, or Northern Ireland, or to Police Scotland on 101 (https://www.scotland.police.uk/contact-us/non-emergencies/) if you are in Scotland. You can also contact your local consumer service: Citizens Advice consumer helpline on 0808 223 1133 in England and Wales, Advice Direct Scotland on 0808 800 9060 in Scotland, or Consumerline on 0300 123 6262 in Northern Ireland. If you believe your identity has been misused, register with Cifas Protective Registration at cifas.org.uk to add a note to your credit file.

Frequently asked questions

Is a message from 'snapchat-support' or 'snapchat_help' real?

No. Snapchat's official support account is verified with a blue badge and has the exact username 'snapchat'. Any variation — with hyphens, underscores, or numbers — is a scam. Do not click links in these messages. If you need help, open Snapchat directly and go to Settings > Help > Contact Us.

What should I do if I already gave a scammer my Snapchat password?

Change your password immediately in the official Snapchat app (Settings > Username > Password). Then enable two-factor authentication (Settings > Two-Factor Authentication) and check your Login Activity to see if anyone else has accessed your account. If the scammer has already changed your password or linked a payment method, contact Snapchat support through the app and explain what happened.

Can I get my money back if I sent it to a Snapchat scammer?

It depends on how you sent it. If you used a bank transfer, contact your bank immediately — they may be able to recall the payment if it hasn't been withdrawn. If you used a gift card or credit card, report it to your card issuer and ask them to cancel the card. If you sent cryptocurrency or used a money transfer service like Western Union, recovery is extremely unlikely. Report the scam to Report Fraud (0300 123 2040 in England, Wales, and Northern Ireland) or Police Scotland on 101 (in Scotland) as soon as possible.

Someone I met on Snapchat is asking me to send money — is this a scam?

Almost certainly yes. Scammers build relationships over weeks or months, then create an urgent reason for you to send money (a business opportunity, a medical emergency, or a way to 'unlock' profits). If someone you've just met is asking for cash, especially if they're pushing you to move to a private chat app or asking for personal details, stop communicating and block them. Do not send money.

What is a Snapchat verification code scam?

Scammers may ask you to share your two-factor authentication code or recovery codes, claiming they need them to 'verify' your account or help you regain access. Never share these codes with anyone. Snapchat staff will never ask for them. If someone asks for your verification code, they are trying to take over your account.

Think you’ve spotted a scam? Use the AI scam checker for an automated second opinion, or report it to Report Fraud for England, Wales and Northern Ireland, or Police Scotland on 101 for Scotland.
